Title: Rome in World Time, Part 11: The Eastern Empire Fights Back (AD 476–1025)

Summary: The Roman Empire did not end in 476. From Constantinople, its emperors reconquered Africa and Italy under Justinian, survived plague, riots and a near-fatal war with Persia, then lost Syria, Egypt and Africa to the Arab conquests and held on through two sieges of the capital. By 1025, under Basil II, it was again the strongest state in Christendom. Over the same five centuries, Islam rose and spread, Tang China flourished and fell, Charlemagne claimed the title of Roman emperor, the Maya collapsed, and Norse sailors reached North America.

---

People who lived in what we call the "Byzantine Empire" never used that name. They called themselves **Romans** (*Rhomaioi*) and their state the Roman Empire. Their neighbours did too: Arabs and Turks called them *Rum*. The word "Byzantine" was popularised by western scholars in the 1500s. This post and the next follow these Romans to the end.

## Zeno to Justinian (476–565)

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 476–491 | **Zeno**. Faces a palace coup by **Basiliscus** (475–476) and a revolt by the generals **Illus and Leontius** (484–488) |
| 488–493 | Zeno sends **Theodoric** and his Ostrogoths to Italy; Theodoric kills Odoacer at a banquet in Ravenna (493) and rules Italy for 33 years |
| 491–518 | **Anastasius I** fills the treasury. Isaurian War (491–497); war with Persia (502–506) |
| **513–515** | **Vitalian**, a general, revolts three times and leads armies to the walls of Constantinople |
| 518 | **Justin I**, an illiterate peasant soldier, becomes emperor; his nephew **Justinian** is the power behind him |
| 527 | **Justinian** becomes emperor, with his wife **Theodora**, a former actress |
| 529–534 | The **Corpus Juris Civilis**: Roman law is codified. It is still the basis of law in much of Europe |
| 530 | Belisarius beats the Persians at **Dara** |
| **Jan 532** | **Nika riots**: the Blue and Green chariot-racing factions unite against the government, burn much of the city and proclaim a new emperor. Theodora tells Justinian that "royalty is a good burial shroud." Belisarius and Mundus trap the crowd in the Hippodrome; Procopius says 30,000 died |
| 532–537 | **Hagia Sophia** is built; dedicated 27 December 537 |
| **533–534** | **Belisarius** destroys the Vandal kingdom with about 15,000 men; Africa is Roman again |
| 535–554 | **Gothic War** in Italy, nearly 20 years of fighting that wrecks Italy |
| **536–537** | **Mutiny in Africa**: soldiers under **Stotzas** revolt and nearly take Carthage |
| 536 | A volcanic "dust veil" darkens the sun for over a year across Europe and Asia |
| 537–538 | The Goths besiege Belisarius in Rome for a year |
| 540 | Belisarius takes **Ravenna**. Persia's **Khosrow I** sacks **Antioch** |
| **541–549** | **Plague of Justinian** (bubonic plague). In 542 it kills perhaps thousands a day in Constantinople |
| 541–552 | Ostrogoth king **Totila** retakes most of Italy, including Rome (546 and 550) |
| 552 | The eunuch general **Narses** kills Totila at Busta Gallorum |
| c. 552 | Monks smuggle **silkworm eggs** from Central Asia; the empire starts its own silk industry |
| 552–554 | A Roman foothold in southern **Spain** is won |
| 562 | Fifty-Year Peace with Persia (it lasts ten) |
| 565 | Justinian dies. The empire is at its largest since 395, and exhausted |

## Near-death and the Arab conquests (565–717)

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 568 | The **Lombards** invade Italy; most of it is lost within a few years |
| 572–591 | Long war with Persia. Emperor **Maurice** (582–602) ends it by restoring the exiled Persian king **Khosrow II** to his throne |
| **602** | The Danube army **mutinies** when ordered to winter across the river. The centurion **Phocas** takes Constantinople and executes Maurice after making him watch his sons killed |
| 602–628 | Khosrow II invades to "avenge" Maurice: the last and greatest Roman–Persian war |
| 608–610 | Revolt from Africa: **Heraclius** sails to Constantinople, kills Phocas and becomes emperor |
| 613–619 | Persia takes Antioch, Damascus, **Jerusalem** (614, carrying off the True Cross) and **Egypt** (618–619) |
| **626** | **Siege of Constantinople** by Avars and Slavs on the European side, with a Persian army across the Bosporus. The city holds |
| 627 | Heraclius, allied with the Khazars, crushes the Persians near the ruins of **Nineveh** |
| 628–630 | Khosrow II is overthrown and killed; Heraclius returns the True Cross to Jerusalem |
| 634 | Arab Muslim armies invade Palestine and Syria |
| **Aug 636** | **Yarmouk**: the Roman army is destroyed. Syria is lost |
| 637/638 | **Jerusalem** surrenders to Caliph Umar |
| 640–642 | **Egypt** is lost; Alexandria surrenders |
| 655 | Battle of the Masts: the Arab navy beats the Roman fleet |
| 663 | **Constans II** visits Rome, the last emperor to do so for over 700 years (until John V in 1369), and strips bronze from the Pantheon |
| 668 | Constans II is murdered in his bath at Syracuse; a usurper, Mezezius, is proclaimed and crushed |
| **674–678** | First Arab siege of Constantinople. **Greek fire**, a liquid incendiary weapon, helps break it |
| 680–681 | The **Bulgars** settle south of the Danube; Rome recognises their state |
| 695 | **Justinian II** is overthrown and his nose is cut off |
| 698 | **Carthage** falls to the Arabs. A navy mutiny makes Tiberius III emperor |
| 705 | Justinian II returns with a Bulgar army and a golden nose; killed in 711 |
| 711–717 | Anarchy: three emperors in six years |
| **717–718** | Second Arab siege. **Leo III** holds the city; the Arab army and fleet are destroyed by winter, disease and Greek fire |

## Iconoclasm, Bulgars and recovery (717–1025)

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| c. 726–730 | Leo III begins **Iconoclasm**, the destruction of religious images (to 787, and again 815–843) |
| 740 | Akroinon: Leo beats an Arab army in Anatolia |
| 742–743 | **Artabasdos** seizes the throne from Constantine V for over a year |
| 751 | The Lombards take **Ravenna**; Rome's power in north Italy ends. The Pope turns to the Franks |
| 797 | Empress **Irene** blinds her son Constantine VI and rules alone |
| **25 Dec 800** | The Pope crowns **Charlemagne** "Emperor of the Romans" in Rome. Constantinople sees it as an insult |
| **811** | **Pliska**: Bulgar Khan **Krum** kills Emperor Nikephoros I and makes his skull into a drinking cup |
| 812 | Constantinople recognises Charlemagne as an emperor (but not "of the Romans") |
| 820 | Leo V is murdered in Hagia Sophia on Christmas Day |
| **821–823** | **Thomas the Slav** leads a huge revolt and besieges Constantinople for over a year |
| 826–827 | Muslim exiles from Spain take **Crete**; Arabs begin conquering **Sicily** (finished in 902) |
| 838 | The Abbasid caliph sacks **Amorium**, home city of the ruling dynasty |
| 843 | Icons are restored ("Triumph of Orthodoxy") |
| **860** | The **Rus** raid the suburbs of Constantinople for the first time |
| 863 | **Cyril and Methodius** begin their mission to the Slavs; the alphabet named after Cyril follows |
| 864–870 | Bulgaria accepts Christianity from Constantinople |
| 867 | **Basil I** murders his patron and founds the **Macedonian dynasty** |
| 904 | Arab raiders sack **Thessalonica** |
| 913–927 | Tsar **Simeon** of Bulgaria tries to take Constantinople; 917 crushing defeat at Achelous |
| 941 | Prince Igor's Rus fleet is burned by Greek fire |
| 957 | Princess **Olga** of Kyiv is baptised in Constantinople |
| 961 | **Nikephoros Phokas** retakes **Crete** |
| 965–969 | Cyprus, Tarsus and **Antioch** (969) are retaken |
| 969 | Nikephoros II is murdered by his nephew **John Tzimiskes**, who takes his throne |
| 971 | Tzimiskes beats **Sviatoslav** of Kyiv at Dorostolon |
| 976 | **Basil II** comes to power |
| **976–979** | Revolt of **Bardas Skleros**, a great general |
| **987–989** | Revolt of **Bardas Phokas**. Basil gets 6,000 Rus warriors from **Vladimir of Kyiv** (the start of the **Varangian Guard**) in exchange for his sister's hand, on condition Vladimir is baptised. Kyivan Rus becomes Christian |
| **29 Jul 1014** | **Kleidion**: Basil crushes the Bulgarians and (by tradition) blinds 15,000 prisoners, leaving one in every hundred with one eye to lead them home. Tsar Samuel dies of shock |
| 1018 | Bulgaria is annexed |
| 15 Dec 1025 | Basil II "the Bulgar-Slayer" dies. The empire stretches from southern Italy to Armenia |

## Things you might not have known happened at the same time

**Heraclius and Muhammad.** Heraclius took the throne in 610, the traditional year of Muhammad's first revelation. While Heraclius was fighting for the empire's life against Persia, Islam was growing in Arabia. By the time he had won, the Arab conquests were about to begin.

**626: the same year Constantinople nearly fell, a Chinese prince killed his brothers to take the throne.** The resulting reign of Tang Taizong became China's model of good government.

**The "Romans" sent an envoy to the Turks in the Altai.** In 568–569, Zemarchus travelled to the Göktürk khan to arrange an alliance against Persia and a silk deal. Rome's diplomacy reached the borders of Mongolia.

**751 was a turning point in three places.** Ravenna fell to the Lombards, the Abbasids beat the Tang at Talas in Central Asia, and the Carolingians took the Frankish throne. Each event redirected a civilisation.

**Vikings reached America during Basil II's reign.** Tree-ring analysis published in *Nature* in 2021 shows Norse settlers cut wood in Newfoundland in 1021. At the same time, other Scandinavians were serving as Basil II's Varangian Guard in Constantinople. Norsemen were at both ends of the known world.

## What comes next

Part 12, the finale: Manzikert, the Crusades, the sack of Constantinople by fellow Christians in 1204, the Nicaean recovery, civil wars, the Ottoman rise, and the final siege of 1453. Meanwhile, the Mongols build the largest land empire in history, Mali's Mansa Musa travels to Mecca, and Gutenberg starts printing.

## Sources and notes

- Procopius, *Wars*, *Buildings* and *Secret History* (Justinian's reign).
- John Malalas, *Chronicle*; Agathias, *Histories*.
- Theophylact Simocatta (Maurice); *Chronicon Paschale*; Theophanes the Confessor, *Chronicle* (to 813).
- Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos, *De Administrando Imperio*; Leo the Deacon; Michael Psellos, *Chronographia* (from 976).
- Al-Tabari, *History of the Prophets and Kings*, for the Arab conquests.
- Anthony Kaldellis, *The New Roman Empire: A History of Byzantium* (2023); Judith Herrin, *Byzantium* (2007).
- Kuitems et al., "Evidence for European presence in the Americas in AD 1021," *Nature* (2021).
- Overview: [Nika riots (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nika_riots), [Battle of the Yarmuk (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Yarmuk), [Basil II (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basil_II), [L'Anse aux Meadows (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%27Anse_aux_Meadows).

**Flags:** Procopius' figure of 30,000 dead in the Nika riots and the 15,000 blinded prisoners after Kleidion are probably exaggerated (Kleidion's number comes from a later chronicler). Death tolls for the Plague of Justinian are heavily debated. The dates for Muhammad's birth and first revelation are traditional. The cause and exact date of Teotihuacan's decline are debated. The year Buddhism officially reached Japan is given as 538 or 552 in different sources.
